module_title: Elastic Load Balancing, Routing and Target Health
review_basis: Individually visually inspected actual Module 08 WebP slides 22–24. Reviewed four CLB panels, four Kubernetes controller panels and four zonal-locality and cost panels.
part_title: Classic Load Balancer, Kubernetes Ingress and Zonal Cost Decisions

scenes.title: Classic Load Balancer — legacy behavior and migration
scenes.visual_overview: Four panels explain Classic Load Balancer listener protocols and certificate limits, pass-through TLS, request distribution and careful migration to modern load balancers.
visual_walkthrough: Upper left: follow HTTP, HTTPS, TCP and SSL listener options; note that CLB lacks SNI, while a certificate can use multiple SAN names
Upper right: trace a TCP listener passing encrypted bytes through for instance-side TLS or mutual TLS; contrast modern ALB client-certificate authentication
Lower left: inspect CLB health probes, HTTP or HTTPS least outstanding requests, TCP round robin and sticky-session imbalance
Lower right: compare cross-zone defaults and migration tests for listeners, certificates, health checks, sessions and rollback
scenes.visual_example: A legacy application on CLB needs to host several HTTPS domain names and preserve client certificates. Inspect certificate SANs and TLS termination design before proposing ALB or NLB migration.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Know CLB to interpret existing environments; choose ALB or NLB for new workloads based on current feature requirements.
scenes.narration: This slide is about understanding a legacy load balancer and knowing when to migrate. In the upper-left, Classic Load Balancer offers HTTP, HTTPS, TCP and SSL listeners. Unlike a modern Application Load Balancer, CLB does not support Server Name Indication, so a single listener certificate may need Subject Alternative Names covering several hosts. Adding names means updating that certificate or separating load balancers. Moving clockwise, the TCP listener can pass encrypted traffic to an instance, allowing that instance to terminate TLS and implement mutual TLS. That is different from an HTTPS listener that terminates TLS at the load balancer, and modern ALB has native client-certificate authentication features. The bottom-left panel compares health-check options and distribution behavior: CLB can probe TCP, SSL, HTTP or HTTPS; HTTP-oriented distribution uses least outstanding requests, whereas TCP uses round robin. Cookie stickiness may help session continuity but can concentrate demand on particular instances. On the bottom-right, the migration illustration reminds us to check cross-zone configuration and deliberately test certificates, connection behavior, session persistence and a rollback path. Imagine a legacy service that needs several HTTPS hosts and client-certificate checking. Rather than assuming a lift-and-shift, decide precisely where TLS must terminate and which ALB or NLB capability replaces the current behavior. The takeaway is that legacy knowledge explains an existing environment but does not make CLB the right choice for a new design.

scenes.title: AWS Load Balancer Controller connects Kubernetes to ELB
scenes.visual_overview: Four panels show Kubernetes resource reconciliation, Ingress-to-ALB and Service-to-NLB mapping, target registration modes, and resource ownership boundaries.
visual_walkthrough: Upper left: read Kubernetes desired-state objects feeding the AWS Load Balancer Controller; it requires scoped IAM rights and suitable subnet discovery
Upper right: distinguish controller-managed Ingress provisioning ALB for HTTP rules from controller-managed LoadBalancer Services provisioning NLB for transport traffic
Lower left: instance targets resolve to node ports, IP targets register pod addresses, and Fargate pods require IP target mode
Lower right: distinguish ingressClass and loadBalancerClass owners and do not overlap controller reconciliation with EKS Auto Mode
scenes.visual_example: An EKS cluster runs an HTTP API on pods and needs host-based routing. Controller-managed Ingress creates ALB routing, while IP target mode can register eligible pod addresses directly; the chosen controller and pod readiness govern reconciliation.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Kubernetes declares exposure, but the selected controller owns AWS resource reconciliation; configure both planes consistently.
scenes.narration: This diagram explains the bridge between Kubernetes desired state and AWS Elastic Load Balancing. Start at the upper-left. The AWS Load Balancer Controller watches supported Kubernetes resources and reconciles the AWS load balancers, listeners, target groups and related settings to match them. That requires correctly scoped IAM permissions and discoverable subnets; a Kubernetes YAML declaration alone cannot create authorized AWS infrastructure. At the upper-right, notice the two Kubernetes entry objects. A controller-managed Ingress ordinarily provisions an Application Load Balancer for HTTP host and path routing. A Service of type LoadBalancer managed by this controller provisions a Network Load Balancer for transport access. These are different intent models, not interchangeable resource names. Now read the lower-left target-mode comparison. Instance mode registers worker node addresses and sends requests through node ports. IP mode instead registers pod IP addresses directly, and pods running on Fargate require this IP model. In either case, the networking rules, readiness probes and target health must agree. The lower-right panel warns about competing ownership. Use the intended ingress class or loadBalancerClass so exactly the desired controller reconciles the resource. Amazon EKS Auto Mode has separate integrated load-balancing capabilities and may require different annotations or settings. For example, a path-routed API on EKS should declare the right Ingress and controller, then validate ALB listeners and healthy pod targets. The architectural lesson is to reason across both the Kubernetes resource layer and the AWS networking layer.

scenes.title: Zonal locality — resilience versus cross-zone transfer
scenes.visual_overview: A regional multi-zone topology with a central compass and cost lens leads into four panels on cross-zone transfer, request path hops, zonal affinity and full service pricing.
visual_walkthrough: Left panel: distinguish ALB and CLB cross-zone balancing transfer treatment from possible inter-AZ charges for NLB and GWLB cross-zone targets
Second panel: trace client-to-balancer, balancer-to-target and later application-to-dependency traffic as separate chargeable or exempt hops
Third panel: consider NLB zonal DNS and supported Resolver zonal-affinity policies, but preserve available serving capacity in every zone
Right panel: calculate complete costs including load-balancer usage or capacity, endpoints, public IPv4, logging and transfer; test AZ failure behavior
scenes.visual_example: A regional application with three Availability Zones considers disabling cross-zone NLB target routing to reduce some transfer charges. Check equal target capacity per zone, DNS steering, recovery when one zone fails and any cross-AZ application database calls before accepting the saving.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Locality is an optimization only if the chosen design still satisfies availability, capacity and failure-recovery requirements.
scenes.narration: The compass and coin magnifier at the center frame a tradeoff: keep traffic local when sensible, but do not compromise availability just to minimize one cost line. Begin with the first lower panel. The slide distinguishes cross-zone load-balancing transfer treatment. Application and Classic Load Balancers do not add regional data-transfer charges for their own cross-zone balancing hop. With Network and Gateway Load Balancers, cross-zone handling can incur inter-Availability-Zone charges depending on the service, configuration and traffic path. The second panel illustrates why hop-by-hop accounting matters. Client to load balancer, load balancer to target, and target to a downstream database or service are separate network paths. An exemption on one hop does not make all application traffic free. In the third panel, zonal DNS naming or supported Route 53 Resolver zonal-affinity policies can influence locality. But if cross-zone routing is disabled, you must ensure every serving zone has healthy capacity and a workable failure strategy. The final panel expands the budget to load-balancer usage or capacity units, associated endpoints, public IPv4, logging and transfer. Consider a three-zone service trying to reduce transfer costs by keeping NLB traffic inside its originating zone. That could help, but only after validating zone-by-zone capacity, expected DNS behavior and an Availability Zone failure. Use current regional pricing and realistic traffic models. The exam lesson is to prefer a sound resilient architecture, then optimize data locality without breaking its requirements.
